title: Scenario 1: The agitated patient
setup: A 34-year-old man is brought to a hospital emergency room by his sister. He is severely agitated, says he will hurt himself, and refuses any treatment. His chart shows a notarized advance directive that states he does not want to be physically restrained unless there is no alternative.

steps.prompt: What is the first thing the team should do about his refusal?

options.text: Treat it as a psychiatric emergency and start restraint right away, since he has refused.
options.feedback: Refusal alone does not trigger the exception. Informed consent is the rule, and the exception requires an emergency or impaired capacity plus four safeguards.

options.text: Check whether this is a psychiatric emergency or whether his capacity is impaired, and assess it through a mental health professional.
options.feedback: Capacity is presumed. Treatment without consent is allowed only in a psychiatric or neurologic emergency or when capacity is impaired.

options.text: Ask his sister to sign consent for everything.
options.feedback: A relative is not automatically the decision maker. A legal representative acts as substitute decision maker only when a professional assesses temporary impairment of capacity.

steps.prompt: The attending professional concludes it is an emergency. What about the advance directive?

options.text: Ignore it, because emergencies override everything.
options.feedback: The intervention must follow the advance directive if one is available.

options.text: Follow it, unless doing so would pose an immediate risk of serious harm to him or another person.
options.feedback: That is the exact exception to following the directive in Section 13.

options.text: Follow it only if his sister agrees.
options.feedback: The directive is the user's own decision; the family's agreement is not the test.

steps.prompt: Restraint is ordered. Which set of safeguards applies?

options.text: It is limited to what is necessary and lasts only while the emergency lasts; the attending professional orders it; the internal review board reviews it within 15 days and every 15 days after; it follows approved guidelines and is fully documented.
options.feedback: These match the safeguards listed in Section 13.

options.text: Any nurse may order it, and review happens at the next annual audit.
options.feedback: It must be ordered by the attending mental health professional, and review is every 15 days.

options.text: It continues until the family collects him, with no review.
options.feedback: It must end when the emergency or impairment ends, and it is reviewed.

steps.prompt: Afterward, the man asks to see his clinical record. What applies?

options.text: He has access to his own records unless the attending professional believes disclosure would cause harm, and he can contest that with the internal review board or the CHR.
options.feedback: That is the Section 5 provision on access to records.

options.text: Records belong to the hospital and are never shared with patients.
options.feedback: Service users have a right of access, subject to the harm exception.

options.text: Only his sister may see them.
options.feedback: Records are his; disclosure to others needs his written consent outside the five exceptions.

title: Scenario 2: The employer's question
setup: An employee receives outpatient care at a clinic. Her manager phones the clinic, saying he is worried and asks what her diagnosis is and whether she will return to work.

options.text: Give the diagnosis, since the manager is concerned about her welfare.
options.feedback: Disclosure needs written consent except in five cases. Concern does not make the call one of them.

options.text: Decline to disclose unless she has given written consent or one of the five exceptions applies.
options.feedback: Confidentiality of records is a right; disclosure needs written consent except for law or court order, the user's consent, a life-threatening emergency, suspected child abuse of a minor, or a case against a professional.

options.text: Confirm only that she is a patient.
options.feedback: Even confirming she is a patient is information about her care and should not be shared without consent.

steps.prompt: What risk does the clinic face if it discloses without a valid basis?

options.text: None, because only courts can penalize.
options.feedback: The Act itself makes violation of confidentiality punishable.

options.text: Imprisonment of six months to two years, a fine of P10,000 to P200,000, or both, falling on the responsible individuals if the facility is a juridical person.
options.feedback: This is the Section 44 penalty clause.

options.text: A written reminder only.
options.feedback: The Act specifies criminal penalties.

steps.prompt: What should the employer be doing, according to the Act?

options.text: Developing workplace mental health policies and programs, correcting stigma and discrimination, and supporting employees with mental health conditions.
options.feedback: This is Section 25. The Civil Service Commission and DOLE have their own duties in Section 35.

options.text: Asking for diagnoses so it can plan.
options.feedback: Support does not require disclosure of diagnoses.

options.text: Nothing; the Act covers only health facilities.
options.feedback: The Act places explicit duties on workplaces.

title: Scenario 3: A municipality starts community mental health
setup: A municipal health officer is asked to start community-based mental health services. The municipality has barangay health workers, two nurses, one physician and a rural health unit. There are no psychiatrists.

options.text: Wait for the DOH to issue operational guidelines before doing anything.
options.feedback: AO 2025-0028 notes that DOH operational guidelines are still to be developed, but LGUs are expected to develop strategies now, with DOH technical assistance.

options.text: Through the local mental health council or local health board: situational analysis and resource mapping, then a CBMH Action Plan using Annex D integrated into the LIPH.
options.feedback: This follows the governance and community engagement provisions.

options.text: Hire a psychiatrist first, then plan.
options.feedback: The framework relies on task sharing and tiered competencies, not only specialists.

options.text: BHWs and others at the Basic tier (awareness, red flags, screening, referral); nurses at the Intermediate tier (assessment, psychoeducation, medication provision, referral); physicians at the Advanced tier (management, treatment).
options.feedback: This is the Annex E tier structure.

options.text: Only physicians may do anything, including screening.
options.feedback: Basic tier services include BHWs and other stakeholders.

options.text: BHWs may prescribe medication.
options.feedback: Medication provision sits at the Intermediate tier and above, delivered by nurses and physicians.

steps.prompt: A patient needs care beyond what the rural health unit can provide. What should happen?

options.text: Refer through the Health Care Provider Network to a higher level, and arrange continuity of care back in the community afterward.
options.feedback: Referral works up and back down, with recovery assistance such as housing, jobs and meaningful daily activity.

options.text: Discharge the patient with no follow-up.
options.feedback: Continuity of care is a key CBMH element.

options.text: Send the patient to the CHD office.
options.feedback: CHDs give technical assistance and monitor; they are not the referral destination.

steps.prompt: What does the municipality owe in reporting?

options.text: Quarterly reports using the Annex F indicators, due in April, July, October and January, with patient data recorded in the MHIS and sharing only under a Data Sharing Agreement.
options.feedback: These are the monitoring and evaluation provisions.

options.text: One annual report in December.
options.feedback: Reporting is quarterly.

options.text: No reporting until a dedicated budget is released.
options.feedback: The order states no dedicated budget; agencies allocate funding within their mandates.
